# Adulthood: working life & activity

> *In the working decades, growth is finished, and the nutritional priority becomes maintenance: keeping
> muscle and holding weight steady while work, the hawker centre and the clock shape most meals.
> Midlife weight gain is usually blamed on a slowing metabolism, but size-adjusted energy expenditure
> barely changes in these years; the levers are activity, muscle, the food environment and a few small
> habits.*

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning objectives
- Explain why a slowing metabolism accounts for little of midlife weight gain, and what drives adult
  weight creep instead.
- Explain why protein maintains muscle mass only alongside resistance exercise, and state the protein range
  for an active adult.
- Match exercise fuelling and hydration to the training load, recognising when ordinary food and
  water are enough.
- Describe how eating out, shift work, stress and short sleep shape the working adult's diet, and the
  evidence for daytime-weighted eating.
- Explain why alcohol has no established safe level and why the heart-protection claim does not hold
  up.
- Recognise the alcohol flush, hazardous drinking, disordered eating and repeated crash dieting, and
  screen, advise or refer.
:::

## Adulthood at a glance: two drivers {#sec-overview}

The healthy working-age adult, from roughly the twenties to the fifties, has moved from building the
body to maintaining it, and sits between adolescence and the midlife and older years (see the
[*Childhood & adolescence*](childhood-adolescence.qmd),
[*Menopause & midlife health*](menopause-midlife.qmd) and [*Healthy ageing*](healthy-ageing.qmd)
chapters). Two topics set this stage apart: fuelling an active body, and eating well inside a working
life.

As at every life stage, the changes fall into two groups:

| Driver | What changes at this stage |
|---|---|
| Internal drivers (inside the body) | Growth is over, so the task is maintenance: maintaining muscle mass against a slow decline, through decades in which the metabolism holds steady |
| External levers (life and environment) | The working-life food environment (the hawker meal, shift work, stress, time scarcity and alcohol) and physical activity, which for the everyday active adult needs far less special fuelling than online advice suggests |

Set a realistic training week in the dial below and see how rarely it calls for more than ordinary
food and water.

<div data-island="fuel-dial" data-src="/diagrams/fuel-dial.yml"></div>

## What changes inside: maintenance, metabolism and muscle {#sec-adult-inside}

### Does metabolism slow down in midlife? {#sec-adult-metabolism}

Midlife weight gain is commonly blamed on a slowing metabolism. Total energy expenditure (the sum of
basal metabolic rate, the thermic effect of food and physical activity; see the
[*Energy balance*](energy-balance.qmd#sec-expenditure) chapter) has been measured with doubly labelled
water across the whole lifespan. Adjusted for body size, it is in fact steady from about 20 to 60. It
does not start falling in the thirties, and declines only later in life [@pontzer2021energy]. The
familiar explanation, "my metabolism is slowing down", therefore accounts for little of midlife weight
gain.

**Weight creep**, the slow adult weight gain of roughly 0.5–1 kg a year, comes instead from a small,
chronic energy surplus, which usually arises from falling activity and muscle plus a little more
intake, not from a falling resting metabolism [@hill2009energygap]. The fixes therefore lie in staying
active, keeping muscle and managing the food environment; a crash diet aimed at a metabolic decline
targets a cause that is not there. Activity alone, however, is a fairly weak lever on weight
once excess has accumulated, so preventing the surplus works better than trying to out-exercise it
later (the clearest data are in women) [@lee2010pawomen].

### Maintaining muscle mass: resistance exercise and protein {#sec-adult-muscle}

Adulthood is about keeping the muscle that growth built. Muscle mass is fairly stable from the late
teens to about 60, drifting down only slowly, and strength fades faster than size
[@mitchell2012sarcopenia]. The popular "you lose 1% a year from thirty" overstates the mid-adult loss,
but the direction is real. These decades are therefore the window to build a reserve before the
steeper losses of older age (see the *Healthy ageing* chapter). Muscle is also the main site of glucose
disposal after a meal [@merz2020muscleinsulin], so keeping muscle protects metabolic health upstream
(for the mechanism, see the [*Integrative metabolism*](integrative-metabolism.qmd#sec-fed) chapter).

Two factors maintain muscle mass, and the second depends on the first. **Resistance exercise**
(muscle-strengthening exercise against a load) is the necessary stimulus: guidelines ask for it on two
or more days a week [@bull2020whopa], muscle gain rises with weekly training volume
[@schoenfeld2017rtvolume], and regular muscle-strengthening is linked to lower risk of death and major
chronic disease [@momma2022strengthmortality]. Protein is the second
factor, but without that stimulus it does little.

The adult protein reference is the **Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA)**, a population reference
intake that is adequate for nearly all healthy adults: about 0.8 g/kg/day (see the
[*Macronutrients*](macronutrients.qmd) chapter). The RDA is a floor, not an optimum: an adult training to build or hold muscle does better at around 1.2–1.6 g/kg/day, and the benefit plateaus near there, so
more is not better [@morton2018proteinmeta]. The range is illustrative, not a number to titrate: an
ordinary diet reaches it, and for most people it means some protein at each meal. The evidence answers
three common worries about protein:

- Timing around a workout barely matters once daily protein intake is adequate; the **anabolic window**
  (the period after exercise in which protein is claimed to be best used) is far wider than the
  supplement industry implies [@schoenfeld2013timing], so food does the job without a powder or a
  30-minute shake.
- Higher intakes are safe for people with normal kidney function; the exception is established kidney
  disease (see the [*Chronic kidney disease*](chronic-kidney-disease.qmd) chapter)
  [@devries2018kidney].
- Plant and animal protein differ little for muscle once the total is adequate; a review found only a
  small edge for animal protein [@lim2021animalplant].

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: a 40-year-old blames her weight gain on a slowing metabolism and plans a crash diet. Why does the plan miss the cause?
Total energy expenditure, adjusted for body size, stays steady from about 20 to 60, so her metabolism
has changed little. Weight creep comes from a small, chronic energy surplus, usually from falling
activity and muscle plus a little more intake. The fixes are staying active, keeping muscle and
managing the food environment. Because activity alone is a fairly weak lever once excess has
accumulated, preventing the surplus works better than trying to out-exercise it later.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: an office worker doubles his protein intake but does no resistance exercise. What happens to his muscle, and why?
Very little changes. Resistance exercise is the necessary stimulus for keeping muscle, and protein
without that stimulus does little. Once the stimulus is in place, about 1.2–1.6 g/kg/day from ordinary
food is enough, and because the benefit plateaus near there, more protein is not better.
:::

## What changes outside: activity, the food environment and alcohol {#sec-adult-outside}

### Fuelling everyday exercise {#sec-adult-fuelling}

Most adults are not training hard, and they need no special sports nutrition: an ordinary healthy
plate and water cover their activity. Sports drinks, gels and protein powders are marketed to everyone
but needed by few, so the practical aim is to guard against over-fuelling.

For adults who do train, fuelling scales with the actual training load, which is usually modest.
Carbohydrate needs rise with training volume (for the fuel physiology of exercise, see the
[*Integrative metabolism*](integrative-metabolism.qmd#sec-exercise) chapter). The high-carbohydrate
and during-exercise fuelling advice, however, is calibrated for serious endurance athletes training for
hours at a time, and does not apply to recreational exercisers [@thomas2016nutritionathletic]. Below
that volume, the advice is simpler:

- A 30–60-minute gym or park session needs water, not a sports drink.
- Hard, once-daily training is met by eating enough overall and getting adequate protein across the
  day, without a special shake.
- Recovery needs only a normal next meal, unless training twice in one day.

Caffeine, the working adult's staple, is a separate question: a coffee before exercise is a mild,
legitimate performance aid, and the concern with bubble tea, energy drinks and kopi is their sugar and
energy content, not the caffeine itself.

::: {.callout-tip}
## 🍜 Hydration in the Singapore heat
The tropics change the advice in one place, fluid. For outdoor exercise or a sweaty commute:

- Drink to thirst, and aim to lose less than about 2% of body weight over a long session, because Singapore's heat and humidity raise sweat losses for the same effort; weighing
  before and after a long run shows the real losses [@sawka2007fluid].
- Add salt only for long or very sweaty sessions (beyond a couple of hours); for a typical workout,
  plain water is right.
- Avoid **drinking far more than is sweated out**, especially plain water over hours: it can cause
  exercise-associated hyponatraemia, a dangerously low blood sodium, so more is not safer
  [@sawka2007fluid].

(For the body-water and sodium physiology behind these rules, see the
[*Micronutrients, hydration and electrolytes*](04-micronutrients-hydration.qmd) chapter.)
:::

### The working-life food environment {#sec-adult-food-environment}

For most adults, diet is shaped less by the home kitchen than by where and when work lets them eat.
Three forces dominate.

**Eating out is the default.** In Singapore the great majority of adults eat out regularly, and many
have a hawker meal every day, chosen for convenience and price [@naidoo2017eatingout]. The hawker
plate, not the home recipe, is therefore the real lever, and counselling around it is a skill of
its own (see the [*What a healthy diet looks like*](dietary-guidelines-patterns.qmd) and
[*Assessing diet and talking to patients*](06-dietary-assessment.qmd) chapters).

**Shift work disrupts circadian rhythms.** Night-shift work is associated with higher rates of type 2
diabetes and metabolic syndrome (a cluster of central fat, hypertension, raised blood glucose and
abnormal blood lipids). These associations come from observational data and are not proof; the
mechanism runs through **circadian misalignment** (eating, sleeping and working out of step with the
body's internal clock) [@xie2024nightshiftt2dm; @sooriya2022shiftmets].

The most useful evidence-aligned change for shift workers concerns when to eat. In a controlled trial,
keeping the main meals in the daytime and avoiding heavy eating in the small hours (roughly midnight to
dawn) prevented the glucose intolerance of simulated night work [@chellappa2021daytimeeating]. More
generally, late-weighted eating is less favourable than an earlier-weighted pattern, though much of
that evidence is observational [@stonge2017mealtiming].

**Stress and short sleep change intake.** Stress nudges intake toward less healthy food
[@hill2022stresseating]. Short sleep, a chronic deficit for many working adults, raises energy intake,
and extending sleep brings it back down [@alkhatib2017sleep; @tasali2022sleepextension], so improving
sleep is also a nutrition intervention.

### Alcohol: cancer and cardiovascular risk {#sec-adult-alcohol}

Clinical advice on alcohol has reversed within a decade. There is no established safe level of
drinking for health: alcohol is a **Group 1 carcinogen** (an agent classed as an established cause of
cancer in humans) that causes at least seven cancers, including breast and oesophageal cancer, and a
meaningful share of alcohol-related cancers arise at light-to-moderate drinking
[@anderson2023nosafelevel; @who2023nosafelevel; @jun2023alcoholcancer].

The belief that "a daily glass of red wine protects your heart" does not hold up. The apparent benefit
came largely from comparing drinkers with a group of "abstainers" that included people who had stopped
drinking because they were ill; **Mendelian randomisation** studies, which use genetic variants to
remove that bias, find no cardiovascular protection, and harm that rises even at low intake
[@piano2025ahaalcohol; @biddinger2022mralcohol]. In practice, never advise anyone to drink for their
heart. Alcohol also supplies empty calories (about 7 kcal/g, with no nutrients), and drinkers eat little less to make up for it,
so it stacks on top of an eating-out diet [@traversy2015alcoholobesity].

::: {.callout-warning}
## Is the alcohol flush harmless?
Reddening after a drink, the **alcohol flush**, is often taken as a harmless quirk. The flush marks a build-up of **acetaldehyde**, the carcinogenic breakdown product of alcohol, and people who flush and keep drinking carry a substantially raised risk of oesophageal cancer [@brooks2009aldh2]. About a third of East Asians carry a variant of ALDH2 (aldehyde dehydrogenase 2, the enzyme that clears acetaldehyde) that makes them flush. The flush is therefore a clinical cue: **ask about it, and
advise cutting down.**
:::

For any adult, the clinician's role at this stage is to screen briefly, advise, and refer anyone with
hazardous or harmful use; deeper management sits with addiction services [@uspstf2018alcohol]. The
usual screen is a short questionnaire such as the **AUDIT-C**, the consumption questions of the Alcohol
Use Disorders Identification Test [@bush1998auditc].

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: why does a 40-minute park run need only water, when athlete guidance recommends carbohydrate during exercise?
Muscle glycogen, the limited carbohydrate store, runs out only in long efforts such as a marathon (glycogen
depletion, described in the *Integrative metabolism* chapter). A 40-minute run therefore ends long before
carbohydrate during exercise could help. The high-carbohydrate and during-exercise advice is
calibrated for serious endurance athletes training for hours at a time, whereas a 30–60-minute session
needs only water, with ordinary meals covering the rest. Applying the athlete advice to a few weekly
sessions over-fuels the exerciser.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: comparisons of drinkers with non-drinkers once suggested that light drinking protects the heart. Why did that benefit disappear?
The "abstainer" comparison group included people who had stopped drinking because they were ill, which
made non-drinkers look less healthy than drinkers. Mendelian randomisation studies, which use genetic
variants to remove that bias, find no cardiovascular protection and harm that rises even at low intake.
Alcohol is also a Group 1 carcinogen, so no one should be advised to drink for their heart.
:::

## Recognising trouble, and when to refer {#sec-adult-refer}

Most of the advice above is preventive, but a few patterns call for recognition and, often, referral.

Weight creep matters sooner in Asian adults, who carry cardiometabolic risk at a lower BMI (hence
Singapore's lower BMI cut-offs; see the
[*Obesity & metabolic syndrome*](obesity-metabolic-syndrome.qmd#sec-phenotype) chapter), so even a few
kilograms of creep can cross a threshold. Established obesity and metabolic syndrome are managed as conditions in their own right (see
the [*Obesity & metabolic syndrome*](obesity-metabolic-syndrome.qmd) and
[*Type 2 diabetes*](type-2-diabetes.qmd) chapters).

Repeated crash dieting is the pattern to steer patients away from. Small, sustainable habits and
regular self-weighing modestly help prevent weight gain [@graham2022smallchange;
@zheng2015selfweighing]. **Weight cycling** (repeated weight loss and regain) has been linked to worse
outcomes, but that signal is heavily confounded by illness causing unintentional weight loss
[@zou2019fluctuation]. The link is therefore not proof that dieting itself kills; the practical
reading is "aim for steady, not sawtooth".

Each of the following patterns is a prompt to act at this stage:

| Pattern | Response at this stage |
|---|---|
| Weight creep crossing Singapore's lower BMI cut-offs | Address early with small, sustainable changes |
| Repeated crash dieting | Advise a steady weight through small habits and regular self-weighing |
| Disordered eating or over-training, in adults as well as adolescents | Recognise and refer |
| Hazardous or harmful drinking | Screen briefly, advise, and refer |
| Alcohol flush with continued drinking | Ask about flushing and advise cutting down |

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: weight cycling has been linked to worse health outcomes. Why does that link not show that dieting itself is harmful?
The link is heavily confounded by illness: people who are ill often lose weight unintentionally, so
some of the weight change reflects disease that is already present. The signal therefore cannot show
that dieting itself causes harm. The practical reading is to aim for a steady weight, kept through
small, sustainable habits and regular self-weighing, and to avoid repeated cycles of restriction.
:::

## Is adulthood just "slowing down"? {#sec-close}

No, and believing it leads to the wrong fixes. The metabolism holds steady through these decades; what
changes is that maintenance replaces growth and the environment sets most of the diet. Midlife weight
creep reflects a small, correctable surplus, not a metabolic decline. The levers are therefore activity, muscle and the food environment, worked through a few durable habits. These include resistance exercise with enough protein to keep muscle, better choices at the daily hawker meal, daytime-weighted meals on shifts, enough sleep, and less alcohol, which adds empty calories and has no established safe level. Two messages have changed: most active adults need only ordinary food and water, not sports
nutrition, and no one should drink for their heart.

## The Singapore picture {#sec-singapore}

**The hawker plate is the food environment.** With most adults eating out regularly, the
population-level gaps the National Nutrition Survey flags, notably that about 9 in 10 adults exceed the
recommended limit of 2,000 mg of sodium a day, are built into everyday meals more than into home cooking [@mohNNS2022; @naidoo2017eatingout].
The national tools target this: the Healthier Dining Programme labels lower-calorie hawker options, and
Nutri-Grade grades the drinks, both practical levers to point patients toward [@hdpHawker2017;
@hpbNutriGrade].

**Activity is often built into the commute.** Singapore's physical-activity guidance mirrors the
international target of 150–300 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity a week plus muscle-strengthening on two or more days
[@spag2022; @bull2020whopa]. A large share of the population's activity comes from walking to and from
transport, and the gamified National Steps Challenge nudges it up [@nphs2023; @yao2022stepschallenge].

**Shift work and long hours are common in several sectors.** These include healthcare, transport and
food and beverage, and the long-hours culture normalises convenient, less healthy eating [@leu2023longhours].

**Local guidance caps alcohol intake.** The cap is about two **standard drinks** (about 10 g of alcohol
each) a day for men and one for women, and health messaging now cites the "no safe level" position;
the ALDH2 flush, common in the Chinese-majority population, makes the "ask about flushing" cue
especially useful here [@mohAlcoholLimits2018; @healthhubAlcoholHazards].
